analysis.one_liner: Removes marijuana from the federal list of banned drugs, erases past possession convictions, and reinvests in communities hit hardest by drug enforcement.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a Senate floor vote and died when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would take marijuana off the federal list of banned drugs, ending federal criminal penalties for making, selling, or possessing it. It would wipe out past federal convictions for marijuana use or possession and let people still in prison for marijuana offenses ask a judge to shorten their sentence. It would also pressure states that arrest minorities and low-income people for marijuana at disproportionate rates by cutting their federal law enforcement money, and redirect those dollars plus up to $500 million a year into a fund for job training, reentry services, libraries, and youth programs in communities hurt most by drug enforcement.
analysis.who_benefits: People with federal marijuana convictions would get their records cleared, and people still imprisoned for marijuana offenses could seek resentencing. Communities with heavy drug-arrest records would receive grant money for job training, reentry, libraries, and youth programs. State-legal cannabis businesses would gain a federal legal footing.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People with marijuana convictions and affected communities

how_it_helps.text: Removes marijuana and THC from schedule I of the Controlled Substances Act and eliminates federal criminal penalties for importing, exporting, manufacturing, distributing, or possessing with intent to distribute marijuana.

Directs every federal court to expunge prior convictions for marijuana use or possession, and allows people still serving federal sentences for marijuana offenses to ask for a hearing where the judge may impose a reduced sentence.

Makes states with disproportionate arrest or incarceration rates for marijuana offenses ineligible for federal prison construction and staffing funds and cuts up to 10% of their Byrne law enforcement grants, with the money redirected to a Community Reinvestment Fund for job training, reentry services, expungement costs, libraries, community centers, youth programs, and health education.

Authorizes $500 million per year from fiscal 2018 through 2040 for the Community Reinvestment Fund, and lets individuals sue in federal court to force the Attorney General to apply the funding penalties.

analysis.who_pays: States that continue arresting minorities and low-income residents for marijuana at above-average rates would lose federal prison funding and up to 10% of their federal law enforcement grants. Federal taxpayers would fund the new $500-million-a-year reinvestment program.
analysis.who_pays_short: States with disproportionate marijuana arrests, and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The bill cuts federal law enforcement and prison funding from states with disproportionate marijuana arrest rates, a penalty that would fall on state and local governments and could reduce services in the very communities the bill targets.
The expungement and resentencing provisions cover federal convictions only; the vast majority of marijuana convictions are in state courts and would remain untouched.
The Community Reinvestment Fund is a new $500-million-per-year federal spending authorization with no offsetting revenue, a cost an honest supporter would have to defend.

Removing all federal penalties for manufacturing and distribution, with no licensing or potency limits in the bill itself, left regulation of a legal marijuana market entirely to the states — an approach critics of legalization generally opposed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefits are large and concrete: clearing federal records and sentences, ending federal marijuana prosecution, and funding communities that bore the cost of enforcement. The main weaknesses are that relief reaches only federal convictions (a small share of all marijuana cases) and that the grant cuts could strain state budgets; the new spending is real but modest by federal standards.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never took it up, and it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Cory Booker introduced the Marijuana Justice Act of 2017 in the Senate on August 1, 2017.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day, with no further action in the record.
Six senators (five Democrats and one independent) cosponsored the bill.
The bill received no committee markup, no floor vote, and never passed either chamber before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal marijuana prohibition and the arrest-and-incarceration status quo continued unchanged, so private prison operators, agencies whose funding depends on drug enforcement, and state-legal cannabis sellers' competitors in prohibition states were better off. People with federal marijuana records got no relief.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The prohibition status quo and its beneficiaries

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and delivered introductory remarks when it was introduced.

for.name: 6 Senate cosponsors (5 Democrats, 1 independent)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only support it attracted in the chamber.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee (Chair Chuck Grassley, R-IA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a markup or vote on it.

against.name: Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor during the 115th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All seven supporters were Democrats and one independent; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-run committee and floor agenda gave the bill no votes.

industries.note: Removing marijuana from schedule I would end the federal ban that keeps licensed sellers in legal conflict and bars normal banking and interstate commerce. Ordinary consumers and these businesses both gain from federal legalization.

industries.industry: Private prison and correctional facility operators
industries.note: The bill eliminates federal criminal penalties for marijuana trafficking and cuts federal prison construction and staffing funds, shrinking the pipeline of marijuana incarceration these facilities profit from.
States with disproportionate marijuana arrest rates would lose up to 10% of Byrne law enforcement grants, tying federal aid to arrest patterns and reducing enforcement resources.

industries.industry: Marijuana enforcement contractors and interdiction programs
industries.note: De-scheduling removes the marijuana offense basis for federal interdiction, wiretap authority, and National Forest drug control enforcement that these programs rely on.
